From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation
Abstract. This pilot study examines how users interpret emoji when immediate verbal context is removed.
In a December 2021 Russian-language paper questionnaire, 100 adult participants in a higher-education
setting in Uzbekistan provided open-ended interpretations of the “emotional meaning” of 20 emoji. The
present article offers a secondary pragmatic reanalysis of the surviving material rather than a
reconstruction of the original match/divergence coding as a measure of correctness. Three recurring
patterns are identified: relatively stable semantic cores, pragmatic variation that preserves a core
meaning, and high semantic-pragmatic variability in which users reconstruct evaluations, speech actions,
or broader communicative scenarios. Action-oriented readings such as “I am silent,” “I have nothing to
say,” and “I am not to blame” are especially notable because they emerged despite an affect-oriented
prompt. The findings position decontextualized elicitation as an exploratory baseline for future controlled
comparisons with contextualized emoji use.
Keywords: emoji; internet pragmatics; pragmatic inference; semantic conventionality; decontextualized
interpretation; speech action; meaning variability

From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation 13
1. Introduction
Emoji are standardized graphic characters, but their communicative meanings are not exhausted by
standardization. In digital interaction, they can display affect, calibrate interpersonal stance, modify
illocutionary force, organize turn-by-turn relations, and contribute to the interpretation of multimodal
messages. This functional range has been established across experimental, corpus-based, interactional,
and social-semiotic research (Bai et al. 2019; Sampietro 2019; Flores-Salgado and Witten 2023; Holtgraves
2024). The pragmatic problem is therefore not simply what an emoji 'means' as a graphic item, but how
users infer what it is doing in a particular communicative environment.
Recent work in Internet Pragmatics has pushed this contextual perspective further. Studies have
examined graphical resources in WhatsApp relational practices, the interaction between the Doge emoji
and verbal text in face-work, the strategic use of emoji in politicians' Twitter/X biographies, emoji functions
in TikTok and DouYin compliments, and the role of emoji in negotiating affiliation and taste in TikTok
comment threads (Pérez-Sabater 2025; Wu and Zhang 2025; Maíz-Arévalo 2025; Xie 2026; Zappavigna
2026). Together with the special issue on visual discourses in digital interaction (Sampietro and Pérez-
Sabater 2025), this work shows that emoji interpretation is closely tied to co-text, sequential position,
platform practices, interpersonal relations, and local expectations.
That contextual orientation raises a complementary question: what interpretive possibilities are
available when immediate verbal context is deliberately removed? Decontextualized presentation is not a
simulation of natural digital interaction. It is a diagnostic condition that reduces one major source of
constraint and thereby elicits a range of interpretations documented in the surviving source materials,
drawing on the graphic sign itself, prior usage experience, and broader cultural conventions. Open-ended
responses to emoji and experimental manipulations of emoji ambiguity have already been used to
investigate meaning agreement and interpretive stability (Boutet et al. 2023; Weissman et al. 2023). The
contribution of the present study therefore does not lie in the mere use of isolated stimuli or free
responses.
A directly relevant precedent is Dainas and Herring’s (2021) Understanding Emoji Survey, which
examined how 523 social-media users interpreted the pragmatic functions of emoji in Facebook comment
contexts. Existing research therefore covers both meaning agreement for isolated emoji and pragmatic
interpretation in situated discourse. Less attention has been paid to how open-ended interpretations
move from affective labeling toward interactional action when immediate verbal co-text and a situational
prompt are absent. The present pilot study targets that narrower gap.
14 Kenenbayev Erkin
Instead, the study asks what kind of interpretive work becomes visible in those responses. A
participant may name an affective state, supply an evaluation, infer a stance toward another person, or
reconstruct a speech action such as remaining silent, refusing to speak, listening, or distancing oneself
from responsibility. This difference matters for internet pragmatics because it marks a movement from
semantic labeling toward action-oriented inference. When a respondent glosses an emoji as “I have
nothing to say” rather than “neutral,” the response does more than choose a different emotion word: it
places the graphic sign in an imagined exchange and assigns it a possible conversational function.
The data come from a December 2021 pilot experiment in which 100 adult participants completed
a Russian-language paper questionnaire containing 20 emoji presented without verbal context. The
original response field was headed “Emotional meaning” (Russian: “Эмоциональное значение”), so
participants were not explicitly prompted to identify speech acts or pragmatic functions. The present
article is a secondary pragmatic reanalysis of the surviving material rather than a retrospective claim that
the current research questions guided the original data collection. The surviving documentation is
incomplete: an individual-level response matrix and a full coding protocol are no longer available, and the
original coding was conducted by one researcher. For that reason, the article does not attempt inferential
statistics or reconstruct the original binary coding as if it were a fully reproducible dataset. The analysis is
deliberately qualitative and descriptive, with the historical match/divergence figures retained only as
secondary descriptive information.
The study addresses three research questions:
RQ1. What patterns of semantic stability and variability are visible in the preserved responses to emoji
presented without immediate verbal context?
RQ2. What types of pragmatic extension appear in users’ open-ended interpretations?
RQ3. For which stimuli do the preserved responses shift from affect labeling toward evaluations, speech
actions, or broader communicative scenarios?
2. Theoretical framework
2.1. Conventionality, ambiguity, and pragmatic inference
Research on emoji has moved well beyond the idea that they are visual equivalents of a small
inventory of emotions. A systematic review by Bai et al. (2019) documents research on semantic
interpretation, emotional expression, individual and cultural differences, platform effects, and social
functions. Manganari (2021) likewise emphasizes the dependence of emoji use and interpretation on
communicative setting and user-related factors. Experimental evidence further shows that emoji differ
From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation 15
substantially in meaning agreement: some items are interpreted with high consistency, whereas
others support much broader distributions of meanings (Weissman et al. 2023).
Conventionality is therefore gradient rather than all-or-nothing. Visual resemblance can support an
interpretation, but prior use, familiarity, and platform-specific conventions also matter. O’Boyle and Doyle
(2023), for example, show that interpretations of WeChat-specific emoji are shaped by use and familiarity
rather than iconically recoverable content alone. Boutet et al. (2023) demonstrate that changes in visual
facial cues can reduce or increase ambiguity in the interpretation of facial emoji. These findings are
important for the present study because a free response that differs from a reference label need not
indicate failure to recognize the image. It may instead reveal a different degree of conventionalization or
a different inferential route from visual form to communicative meaning.
Yus (2025) frames emoji explicitly as a pragmatic problem, focusing on the inferential work involved
both when emoji modify verbal material and when they occur without accompanying text. The latter case
is especially relevant here. With fewer immediate contextual constraints, users must rely more heavily on
stored conventions, salient visual features, memories of previous uses, and assumptions about plausible
communicative situations. The resulting interpretation is not context-free in an absolute sense: users
always bring background knowledge and usage histories to the task. 'Decontextualized' in this article
therefore means that the experiment supplied no immediate verbal co-text or scenario, not that
interpretation took place without social or cognitive context.
This distinction also clarifies why technical names and pragmatic interpretations should not be
conflated. Unicode and CLDR provide standardized identifiers and short names needed for interoperable
digital representation. Those labels are indispensable for identifying a stimulus, but they are not
comprehensive descriptions of the social, interpersonal, or illocutionary functions users may infer in actual
communication. The present study treats such technical labels as identification tools, while treating the
open responses as evidence about possible user-level interpretations.
2.2. From affect labeling to speech action
A major strand of pragmatic research concerns what emoji do in interaction. Sampietro (2019)
shows that emoji in Spanish WhatsApp chats can strengthen or mitigate illocutionary force, support
openings and closings, and contribute to playful relational work. Flores-Salgado and Witten (2023)
demonstrate that graphicons in Mexican parent-school WhatsApp communities accompany speech acts,
help organize interaction, and can sometimes substitute for verbal material. Holtgraves (2024) moves the
issue directly into experimental pragmatics by asking whether single emoji can be used to perform
16 Kenenbayev Erkin
speech acts. Across four experiments, participants were able to associate particular emoji with
intended actions, although senders could overestimate how successfully recipients would identify those
actions.
These findings provide a useful distinction for the present data. Some free responses describe an
internal state: “anger,” “sadness,” “confusion,” or “joy.” Other responses are more interactional: “I am
silent,” “I am listening,” “I have nothing to say,” “I am not to blame,” or “my lips are sealed.” Such
formulations presuppose an imagined speaker, addressee, or prior event. They can be analytically
interpreted as construing the graphic stimulus as a compressed move in a possible exchange. The analytical
question is therefore not only which emotion is named, but whether the response remains at the level of
affect or moves toward stance and action.
For this reason, the qualitative reanalysis distinguishes three interpretive orientations. The first is
affective or descriptive labeling, in which the response names a state or visible expression. The second is
evaluative or interpersonal stance, in which the response attributes irony, disapproval, friendliness,
embarrassment, distrust, or another relational position. The third is action/scenario construal, in which
the respondent infers a possible speech act, conversational move, or larger situation. These orientations
are not claimed to be mutually exclusive psychological categories. They are descriptive tools for tracing
how far an interpretation moves from visual labeling toward interactional inference.
2.3. Context as a constraint on emoji interpretation
Experimental and interactional research makes clear that verbal context can guide emoji
interpretation. Scheffler et al. (2022) show that emoji used as word substitutions are processed in relation
to their sentence context, while Dai et al. (2024) demonstrate interactions between textual and emoji
valence. Gibson (2024), analyzing Tinder chats, shows that even context does not necessarily remove
ambiguity: the meaning of a winking emoji depends on sequential position, idiosyncratic usage, and the
ambiguity of the verbal action with which it co-occurs.
Recent work in Internet Pragmatics similarly treats visual resources as parts of multimodal
interaction rather than isolated symbols. Pérez-Sabater (2025) identifies relational functions of graphical
elements in large WhatsApp corpora. Wu and Zhang (2025) show how the Doge emoji and verbal co-text
combine in face-work. Maíz-Arévalo (2025) analyzes how politicians balance professional and friendly self-
presentation through emoji in Twitter/X biographies. Xie (2026) develops a functional taxonomy from
1,000 emoji-containing compliments on TikTok and DouYin, while Zappavigna (2026) examines emoji as
resources for negotiating affiliation and taste in TikTok comments. These studies illustrate the
From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation 17
interpretive narrowing and functional specification that emerge when an emoji is embedded in a
recognizable activity.
The present design approaches the same phenomenon from the opposite direction. By withholding
immediate verbal context, it does not ask how an emoji functions in one observed interaction; it asks what
kinds of plausible interpretive pathways are visible before a particular interaction selects among them. In
that sense, decontextualized interpretation can serve as a baseline for future experiments that compare
the same stimulus across isolated and contextualized conditions. The central hypothesis motivating that
future work is not that context always eliminates ambiguity, but that it redistributes the relative
accessibility of competing interpretations.
3. Method
3.1. Participants and procedure
The original experiment was conducted in December 2021 as an open-ended linguistic
questionnaire. It involved 100 adult participants aged 19–55 in a pedagogical higher-education setting in
Uzbekistan. The preserved summary documentation identifies 38 fourth-year students, 25 third-year
students, 25 second-year students, and a combined group of 12 master’s students and teachers.
Participants came from Russian-medium and Uzbek-medium educational tracks. The study was not
designed as a representative demographic survey; its purpose was to elicit a range of interpretations of
the same set of graphic stimuli.
The stimulus set contained 20 emoji. All stimuli were presented on the same Russian-language paper
questionnaire rather than on participants’ personal devices, so participant-side platform rendering
differences were not part of the elicitation condition. The surviving questionnaire template contains fields
for the participant’s full name, age, and group, and the response column is headed “Emotional meaning”
(Russian: “Эмоциональное значение”). Participants were therefore not explicitly asked to identify speech
acts or pragmatic functions. Each emoji was shown separately without an accompanying sentence,
dialogue, or situational prompt, and participants wrote their responses in Russian. Responses could consist
of a word, phrase, or short utterance. The English renderings of response examples in this manuscript were
prepared for the present article from the preserved Russian formulations. Because no contextual condition
was included, the design cannot estimate the causal effect of context; it can only document the
interpretive range observed under an isolated-presentation condition.
18 Kenenbayev Erkin
3.2. Stimulus identification and the historical reference frame
The surviving working materials identify stimuli by Unicode code points and CLDR short names. On
the basis of the stimulus inventory and the chronology of emoji releases, the technical frame is
retrospectively reconstructed as Unicode Standard 14.0 / Unicode Emoji 14.0 and CLDR 40.0. This
reconstruction is supported by the presence of U+1FAE0 MELTING FACE, introduced with Emoji 14.0, and
by the fact that CLDR 40 supplied names and search keywords for Emoji 14.0. Unicode 14.0 was released
on September 14, 2021, and CLDR 40 on October 27, 2021 (Unicode Consortium 2021a, 2021b). Because
data collection took place in December 2021, both releases predated the experiment, making the
reconstruction chronologically consistent. The version number itself was not recorded in the surviving
questionnaire, so the identification is still reported as a retrospective reconstruction rather than as an
original procedural record.
The original coding also used expanded Russian-language descriptions as a working comparison
frame. Retrospective checking indicates that many of those formulations closely reproduce or resemble
material from EmojiAll, with some items matching descriptions found on Emojis.wiki and eemojis.ru. These
websites are not normative sources for Unicode semantics. They are cited here only to document the
historical comparison frame used in the experiment. Accordingly, the original categories of 'match' and
'divergence' are not interpreted as correct versus incorrect understanding.
Technical verification also identified two problems in the surviving stimulus table. First, U+1F600
has the CLDR short name GRINNING FACE. Second, stimulus 12 displayed 🤪 and was accompanied by a
description corresponding to ZANY FACE, but the table listed U+1F61C WINKING FACE WITH TONGUE. The
present article uses the corrected identification U+1F92A ZANY FACE. These corrections affect stimulus
documentation, not the preserved participant responses.
3.3. Original coding and present reanalysis
The original 2021 study was framed primarily in terms of interpretive agreement and comparison with a
reference set of emoji descriptions. The source documentation also records exploratory attention to group
membership, duration of shared activity, age, and gender. The present article constitutes a secondary
pragmatic reanalysis of the surviving material. It therefore does not treat the historical comparison frame
as a normative measure of correct emoji understanding and does not retrospectively attribute the present
research questions to the original data-collection design.
In the original analysis, repeated interpretations and responses judged by the researcher to be
synonymous were collapsed into broader meaning categories on the basis of perceived semantic
From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation 19
equivalence. There was no independent second coding and no inter-coder reliability estimate. The
surviving documentation does not include the complete individual response matrix or a full decision log
showing how every response was assigned to a category. The original percentages therefore cannot be
recalculated independently and are used only as descriptive characteristics of the historical coding.
The surviving summary tables distinguish four aggregated participant groups. Their mean
proportions of divergence from the historical working frame are 64%, 67%, 71%, and 60%, respectively,
with an unweighted mean of 65.5%. These percentages are not treated as 2,000 independent observations
(100 participants × 20 stimuli), nor are they used to compare groups statistically. The source materials do
not preserve the individual-level variables needed for balanced analyses by language, age, gender, or
educational level. Retrospective chi-square tests, Fisher exact tests, Cramér’s V estimates, or confidence
intervals would therefore create a false impression of precision.
The present reanalysis shifts the focus from the binary historical coding to the type of variation
visible in the preserved response examples. Because the complete participant-level response matrix is no
longer available, the reanalysis is illustrative rather than exhaustive and does not claim to recover the full
distribution of response types. Three patterns are used as heuristic categories: (1) relatively stable
interpretation, where lexically different responses remain within one broad semantic field; (2) variation
with preservation of a semantic core, where respondents add evaluative or pragmatic nuances without
leaving that field; and (3) high semantic-pragmatic variability, where preserved examples distribute across
competing affective, evaluative, or action-oriented scenarios. The categories are analytic rather than
statistical, and they require future validation on individual-level data coded independently by multiple
researchers.
3.4. Ethics and data status
The surviving study documentation does not contain a separate written informed-consent form or
a record of prior ethics-committee approval. The original questionnaire was not anonymous at the point
of collection: the form contained fields for the participant’s full name, age, and group, and the surviving
source documentation reproduces an example of a completed questionnaire containing identifying
information. Participation was voluntary and involved adult participants aged 19–55 in a non-
interventional linguistic questionnaire; no medical, clinical, biological, or physical intervention was
involved, and no sensitive categories of personal data were collected. The present manuscript reports only
aggregated information and de-identified response examples; no participant names are reproduced.
On 13 October 2026, the institution at which the study was conducted issued an institutional
determination regarding the ethics-review requirements applicable to the study. After reviewing the
20 Kenenbayev Erkin
regulatory and local requirements in force at the time of data collection, the institution determined
that separate prior review and approval by an Ethics Committee / Institutional Review Board was not
required for this type of non-interventional linguistic questionnaire study in 2021. This determination
concerns the applicability of ethics-review requirements and does not constitute retrospective ethics
approval.
The individual response matrix and complete original coding protocol are no longer available. The
retained study materials include the questionnaire template, the preserved visual forms of the 20 stimuli,
grouped summaries, examples of free responses, and completed paper questionnaires retained by the
institution at which the study was conducted. Because the completed questionnaires contain personal
identifiers, they are not transferred to third parties, and any material provided to editors or reviewers
must be de-identified in advance. This data limitation is material: the article does not claim to reconstruct
participant-level distributions that are no longer auditable from the surviving analytical records.
4. Results
4.1. Overall pattern
The surviving source summary reports substantial differences in interpretive stability across the 20
stimuli. It records no complete uniformity of interpretation for any stimulus and notes that some items
generated as many as 15 distinct verbal formulations. This does not mean that all variation was equally
consequential. In some cases, different words pointed to the same broad affective meaning; in others, the
responses moved across different evaluative positions or imagined communicative actions. The latter are
methodologically notable because the original response field asked for “emotional meaning,” not for a
pragmatic function or speech act.
The three-pattern model is therefore based on semantic distance rather than on a fixed percentage
threshold. A low divergence percentage can still contain several lexical variants, while a high percentage
can arise because the historical reference frame was narrow even though the responses remain within
one broad emotional field. The most informative cases are those in which responses cross levels of
construal—for example, from a facial state to an interactional move such as remaining silent or refusing
responsibility.
4.2. Relatively stable semantic cores
The clearest examples of relative stability are U+1F600 GRINNING FACE and U+1F602 FACE WITH
TEARS OF JOY. In the third-year group, the historical divergence figure was 0% for both items, and
From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation 21
responses clustered around meanings such as 'joyful smile,' 'laughter,' 'laughing to tears,' and 'very
funny.' The second-year summary likewise reports 0% divergence for both. In the combined
master’s/teacher group, U+1F600 had 0% divergence and U+1F602 had 10%, with responses such as
'happy smile,' 'laughter to tears,' and 'tears of joy.'
The important point is not the exact historical percentage, but the limited semantic distance among
responses. Participants used different lexical labels, yet these labels generally remained inside a common
affective domain of positive amusement or joy. This is the first pattern: lexical variability without
substantial pragmatic divergence.
4.3. Pragmatic variation within a shared emotional field
U+1F620 ANGRY FACE illustrates a second pattern. The combined master’s/teacher group had a
historical divergence figure of 10%, with responses including 'anger,' 'rage,' and 'aggression.' The third-
year group showed 30% divergence and included 'dissatisfaction' and 'angry face'; the second-year group
reached 50%, but its responses still remained predominantly in a negative-affect field. The variation
therefore often reflects narrowing, strengthening, or reframing of the same broad affective orientation
rather than a move into a wholly different semantic domain.
This pattern matters because a binary match/divergence measure exaggerates the distance
between some responses. A participant who writes 'aggression' rather than 'anger' may be intensifying or
socially reframing a negative affective display rather than construing a different communicative event. The
qualitative reanalysis therefore treats these answers as pragmatic extensions within a shared core.
4.4. High variability and competing pragmatic scenarios
U+1F643 UPSIDE-DOWN FACE produced a markedly different response profile. The surviving fourth-
year summaries contain two subgroup values of 100% and 97% divergence from the historical reference
frame; subgroup sizes are not recoverable from the retained materials and these values are therefore
descriptive only. The third-year, second-year, and master’s/teacher summaries report 90%, 95%, and 90%,
respectively. More important than those figures is the spread of response types: 'playful mood,' 'joy,' 'I do
not want to offend,' 'embarrassed smile,' 'smile with irony,' 'hinting,' 'smile because of guilt,' and 'good
mood.' The interpretations span playfulness, irony, embarrassment, friendliness, guilt, hinting, and
positive affect.
U+1F972 SMILING FACE WITH TEAR shows another kind of competition. The surviving fourth-year
summaries both report 100% divergence; the third-year group also reports 100%, the second-year group
90%, and the master’s/teacher group 100%. Preserved responses include 'boredom,' 'sad face,' 'tear of
22 Kenenbayev Erkin
joy,' 'sympathy,' 'offense,' 'self-irony,' 'guilt,' 'tears of happiness,' and 'tears of disappointment.' The
preserved responses suggest that the combination of smile and tear was compatible with competing
positive, negative, and mixed-affect scenarios. This pattern is consistent with experimental evidence that
small changes in facial cues can materially alter interpretation (Boutet et al. 2023).
U+1F610 NEUTRAL FACE is particularly important for the move from affect to action. The surviving
fourth-year values range from 90% to 100%, the third-year summary reports 90%, and the
master’s/teacher summary 100%. Responses include 'neutrality,' 'confusion,' 'bewilderment,'
'disappointment,' and 'dissatisfied,' but also 'I have nothing to say,' 'I am silent,' 'I am listening,' and
'speechless.' The latter responses do not simply name an emotion. They construe the face as a possible
conversational move or participation stance.
A comparable shift appears with U+1F636 FACE WITHOUT MOUTH and the sequence U+1F636
U+200D U+1F32B U+FE0F FACE IN CLOUDS. For FACE WITHOUT MOUTH, preserved responses range from
relatively literal formulations such as 'my lips are sealed,' 'no words,' and 'silence' to 'confusion,'
'bewilderment,' 'shocked,' and 'I know nothing.' For FACE IN CLOUDS, responses include 'thinking,' 'lost in
thought,' 'fear,' 'confusion,' 'I am not to blame,' 'my brain is boiling,' 'hidden thoughts,' 'fog in my head,'
'hiding,' 'shame,' and 'head in the clouds.' The cloud motif becomes a resource for metaphorical scenario
construction involving cognitive uncertainty, hiding, distraction, self-distancing, or the desire to disappear.
U+1F644 FACE WITH ROLLING EYES likewise supports several interpretive directions. The surviving
fourth-year summaries report 100% and 95% divergence, the third-year group 100%, the second-year
group 90%, and the master’s/teacher group 100%. Responses include puzzlement, irritation, boredom,
distrust, and reflection. The same visible gesture can thus be construed as an internal affective state, an
evaluation of another person’s utterance, or a cognitive response. Table 1 summarizes the principal
contrastive patterns across selected stimuli.

4.5. Three mechanisms of interpretive variability
Taken together, the preserved examples reveal three qualitatively different mechanisms. First, users
may select different lexical labels within a stable semantic core, as with joy and laughter. Second, they
may preserve the core but foreground a different intensity, evaluative nuance, or interpersonal
implication, as with anger, aggression, and dissatisfaction. Third, they may reconstruct an imagined
interactional scenario, as when a neutral or mouthless face becomes “I am silent,” “I have nothing to say,”
or “my lips are sealed.”
The third mechanism is the most pragmatically consequential. It indicates that an isolated emoji can
cue not only an affective concept but a possible action format. This does not show that the emoji would
actually perform the same speech act in real interaction; the experiment did not provide an addressee,
prior turn, or communicative goal. It does show that action-oriented interpretations are
24 Kenenbayev Erkin
available to users even before such context is supplied. Holtgraves’s (2024) experimental findings
on emoji and speech acts make this observation theoretically plausible, while the present data extend the
issue to open-ended, unprompted scenario reconstruction.
5. Discussion
5.1. Emoji differ in interpretive conventionality
The first major finding is that emoji should not be treated as a semantically uniform class. Some
stimuli preserve a relatively stable affective core under isolated presentation, whereas others support
several competing interpretations. This pattern converges with Weissman et al. (2023), who show
substantial variation in meaning agreement across emoji. The present data add a qualitative dimension:
disagreement can arise not only because users choose different labels, but because they construe the sign
at different pragmatic levels.
That distinction helps explain why reference-based mismatch rates are a weak standalone measure.
If one respondent writes 'anger' and another 'aggression,' a binary coding system may mark one answer
as divergent depending on the reference wording, yet both responses occupy a similar negative-affect
field. By contrast, 'I am silent' and 'confused' differ more substantially because one construes an action
while the other construes a state. Pragmatic analysis therefore benefits from examining the semantic
distance and interactional orientation of responses rather than merely counting lexical correspondence.
5.2. From visual state to interactional move
The second major finding concerns the recurrent shift from state description to action-oriented
interpretation. Responses such as “I am silent,” “I am listening,” “I have nothing to say,” “my lips are
sealed,” and “I am not to blame” presuppose a participant role and an imagined conversational
environment. In pragmatic terms, the respondent has supplied missing contextual structure. The graphic
sign becomes a candidate reply, stance display, refusal to speak, or act of self-distancing.
The wording of the original prompt is methodologically important. Participants were explicitly asked for
the “emotional meaning” of each emoji rather than for its pragmatic function. Action- and scenario-
oriented responses therefore emerged despite an affect-oriented elicitation prompt. This makes such
responses particularly informative for the present reanalysis, while also imposing a constraint: the wording
of the prompt may have increased the proportion of affective labels, so the relative frequency of affective,
stance-oriented, and action-oriented responses cannot be treated as a neutral measure of their
availability.
From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation 25
This pattern aligns with work showing that emoji can contribute to illocutionary force and sequential
organization in actual messaging (Sampietro 2019; Flores-Salgado and Witten 2023), and with Holtgraves’s
(2024) finding that users can associate single emoji with particular speech acts. The contribution of the
present pilot data is narrower but complementary: action-oriented interpretations emerged
spontaneously without an instruction to imagine a speech act. This suggests that speech-action construal
is one available route in users’ emoji knowledge.
At the same time, the evidence does not justify a claim that a given emoji intrinsically encodes a
speech act. The same stimulus can cue state, evaluation, and action across different respondents. For
U+1F610 NEUTRAL FACE, for example, 'neutrality,' 'confusion,' and 'I am silent' coexist. The pragmatic
potential of the sign is therefore better described as a structured field of affordances for inference than
as a fixed inventory of encoded acts.
5.3. Decontextualization as a baseline, not a model of natural interaction
The absence of verbal context is both the defining feature and a major limitation of the design. It
increases the space of possible readings, but it does not allow the study to measure how much a specific
context would narrow that space. There was no contextualized control condition, so any claim that context
'reduces ambiguity' in these data would be causal overreach. What the surviving material provides is an
exploratory baseline of documented readings under one restricted elicitation condition.
This baseline is useful precisely because recent internet-pragmatic research documents richly
contextualized emoji functions. In WhatsApp corpora, emoji participate in relational work (Pérez-Sabater
2025); in Bilibili comments, the Doge emoji interacts with verbal politeness strategies in face management
(Wu and Zhang 2025); in social-media profiles, emoji contribute to self-presentation (Maíz-Arévalo 2025);
in compliments, they occupy systematic pragmatic and positional roles (Xie 2026); and in TikTok comment
threads, they help negotiate affiliation and taste (Zappavigna 2026). These studies describe what emoji do
after a concrete activity has constrained interpretation.
The present study asks what remains possible before that constraint is supplied. The answer is not
unlimited interpretation. Grinning and laughing faces still show relatively stable cores. Rather, the baseline
appears to be stimulus-specific: some signs strongly cue a shared affective field, while others—especially
visually ambivalent or interactionally suggestive faces—invite scenario construction. A future within-
participant design can test this claim directly by presenting the same emoji both alone and inside
controlled conversational contexts.
26 Kenenbayev Erkin
5.4. Affective ambivalence and visual configuration
U+1F972 SMILING FACE WITH TEAR illustrates how the preserved responses may reflect competing
construals associated with a visually ambivalent configuration. The smile and tear are compatible with
happiness, relief, sadness, embarrassment, resignation, or mixed affect, and the preserved responses span
both positive and negative interpretations. This is consistent with Boutet et al. (2023), who show that facial
cues can alter interpretive ambiguity, and with more recent work on visual morphology showing that
meaning depends on how conventionalized graphic components combine (Lichtenberg et al. 2026).
The same principle applies in a different form to FACE IN CLOUDS. Here the cloud supports
metaphorical mappings: mental fog, hidden thoughts, cognitive overload, disappearing, shame, or
avoiding responsibility. The interpretation is therefore not a direct recognition of an emotion. It is a small
act of scenario building from a visual configuration. Such cases are particularly useful for pragmatics
because they foreground inference as a constitutive part of emoji meaning rather than as a secondary
correction to an encoded label.
5.5. What the aggregate percentages can and cannot show
The historical group means—64%, 67%, 71%, and 60% divergence, with an unweighted mean of
65.5%—are retained only to document the scale of divergence in the original coding. They cannot support
the statement that '65.5% of users do not know the meaning of emoji,' nor can they establish that one
educational group interprets emoji more accurately than another. They combine decisions made against
a historically narrow reference frame, and the individual response matrix needed to audit those decisions
is unavailable.
For the same reason, the study does not make claims about Russian-medium versus Uzbek-medium
participants, age, gender, or educational level. The source documentation is not sufficiently complete for
balanced subgroup analysis. Any apparent group difference in the surviving summaries should be treated
as descriptive archival information, not as evidence of a population effect. This restriction is important
given the literature showing that emoji interpretation may vary with generation, gender, culture, and
usage experience (Togans et al. 2021; Zhukova and Herring 2024).
6. Limitations and directions for further research
The study is a pilot analysis based on partially preserved documentation from an earlier experiment.
Its strongest limitations are the absence of an individual-level response matrix, the absence of
independent second coding, and the lack of a full coding decision log. The original procedure did not
From Affect to Action: Pragmatic Variability in Decontextualized Emoji Interpretation 27
include a contextualized comparison condition or an a priori power analysis, and the surviving
materials do not document any randomized presentation order. Because all participants saw a paper
questionnaire, participant-side platform rendering differences were avoided. The exact source or vendor
style of the printed emoji artwork is not documented; however, the surviving questionnaire template
preserves the visual forms of the stimuli as presented in the study. These limitations sharply restrict
quantitative inference.
The surviving documentation does not include a separate written consent form or a prior ethics-
approval record. An institutional determination issued on 13 October 2026 by the institution at which the
study was conducted established that separate prior Ethics Committee / Institutional Review Board review
and approval was not required for this type of non-interventional linguistic questionnaire under the
requirements applicable in 2021. The determination concerns the applicability of ethics-review
requirements and does not constitute retrospective ethics approval.
A stronger follow-up study should preserve individual responses and assign them to pre-specified
but revisable coding dimensions. At minimum, two independent coders should classify responses and
inter-coder agreement should be reported. A useful coding architecture would distinguish affect/state
labeling, evaluative or interpersonal stance, speech action, and broader scenario construal, while allowing
multi-label responses where necessary.
The most informative experimental extension would use the same emoji in at least two conditions:
isolated presentation and controlled verbal context. Contexts could be designed to favor different
plausible interpretations of the same emoji, making it possible to estimate how strongly verbal information
narrows or redirects the response space. Platform rendering should be standardized, and the sample
should be balanced in advance if language, age, or other group variables are to be tested. Such a design
would move from the present descriptive baseline toward a direct test of pragmatic constraint.
7. Conclusion
The preserved materials from this pilot study suggest that decontextualized emoji interpretation
varies not only in lexical wording but in the level at which users construe the sign. Some emoji retain a
relatively stable affective core. Others invite evaluative or interpersonal elaboration. A third group
supports broader pragmatic reconstruction, including imagined replies, participation stances, and
communicative scenarios. The distinction between these patterns is more informative than a binary
contrast between 'matching' and 'non-matching' answers.
28 Kenenbayev Erkin
The most theoretically relevant shift is from affect to action. Because the original questionnaire
explicitly asked for “emotional meaning,” responses such as “I am silent,” “I have nothing to say,” “my lips
are sealed,” and “I am not to blame” were not elicited by an instruction to name pragmatic functions. They
supply a missing interactional environment and assign the emoji a possible role within it. Such responses
do not prove that a speech act is encoded in the emoji, but they show that action-oriented inference forms
part of the interpretive repertoire available to users.
For internet pragmatics, the study therefore offers an exploratory baseline perspective
complementary to corpus studies of emoji in situated interaction. Contextual research demonstrates how
verbal co-text, sequential position, platform norms, and interpersonal goals shape actual emoji functions.
Decontextualized elicitation reveals which interpretations remain available before those constraints are
imposed. Future controlled comparisons between isolated and contextualized conditions can test how
pragmatic context selects, suppresses, or reorganizes that interpretive field.
